title: Top-down and bottom-up construction
subtitle: Which direction a garment or accessory is built in, and why it matters
excerpt: Crochet garments can be worked from the top toward the hem (top-down) or from the hem upward (bottom-up). The direction affects how shaping is distributed, where you try on the piece, and how easy it is to adjust length.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet — construction methods. Standard British crochet pattern writing conventions.

glossaryTerms.definition: A garment worked from the neckline or crown downward. The yoke is shaped first; sleeves and body separate at the underarm. Length adjustments happen near the end of the work.
A garment worked from the hem upward. Body and sleeves are made separately and joined at the yoke. Traditional method used in most vintage crochet patterns.

heroPrompt: Two flat crochet swatches on a pale surface showing contrasting construction arrows — one with an arrow pointing downward from the neckline area, one with an arrow pointing upward from the hem, both in cream DK cotton.

content.text: Most crochet patterns specify one direction for construction. Understanding what each direction means makes the shaping instructions legible before you start — instead of following rows blindly and wondering why increases are appearing near the yoke.

the hem is row 1. Front, back, and sleeves are usually worked as separate pieces, then joined at the shoulders by seaming or a three-needle bind-off equivalent. Most vintage and traditionally written British patterns use this method.
Clear waist and bust shaping: increases and decreases appear at predictable row counts.
Length adjustment is straightforward: add or remove rows before the armhole shaping begins.
Seaming required unless the pattern is designed in the round.

the neckline is row 1. The yoke is worked flat or in the round with raglan increases radiating from four points. When the yoke is deep enough, stitches for each sleeve are placed on holders and the body continues to the hem as a tube.
Try on as you go: the piece can be worn on the needles to check yoke depth and sleeve length in real time.
Seamless or nearly seamless: suited to crocheters who dislike finishing seams.
Length adjustments are easy at the body and sleeve ends — add or remove rows before the hem border.

For a first garment, bottom-up gives the simplest shaping logic — you follow a flat piece row by row, and the construction decisions are confined to the shoulder and neckline at the end. Top-down is worth learning once you want to size-adjust on the fly, since trying on mid-work is direct feedback that saves frogging a finished piece.
